teaser: The stone has not left his hand yet. Everything in this giant is the second before.
review_notes:
Reading of the moment as 'before the fight' is the majority view, not unanimous.
Block history: quarried around 1464 for Agostino di Duccio, abandoned; second attempt (Antonio Rossellino, 1476) also abandoned; given to Michelangelo in 1501. Lesson simplifies to 'two sculptors'.
Height 5.17 m including base; weight 'more than five tons'.
January 1504 committee included Leonardo da Vinci and Botticelli. Move in May 1504: four days, about forty men, stones thrown at night: check.
1527: bench thrown from a window of the Palazzo broke the left arm in three pieces. 1873 move to the Accademia; copy in the square since 1910. 1991 hammer attack on a toe of the left foot.
Oversized head and right hand explained by intended high placement: a common hypothesis, presented as such.
Photo is taken from below and slightly to the side in the Accademia tribune; the sling strap itself is barely visible, the find points at the left hand at the shoulder.

lesson.text: Stop the story of David and Goliath one second before the end. The giant is still alive, somewhere off to the side. The boy has stepped forward. He has seen his target and chosen his moment, and his arm has not moved yet. This is the instant Michelangelo carved.

That was a new choice. Florentine sculptors before him had shown David after the kill, a slim boy with a sword and the giant's head at his feet. Here there is no head and no sword. There is not even an enemy. All you get is a naked young man and whatever is going on behind his eyes.
He does carry a weapon, though, and it is easy to miss. Tap where you think it is.

spots.title: The sling
spots.text: The raised left hand holds one end of a sling, a simple strap for hurling stones. It lies over the shoulder and runs down his back to the other hand.

lesson.text: A strap of leather against an armored giant. By hiding it almost completely, Michelangelo moves the fight somewhere else. David will win because he thinks faster and dares more. The statue is a portrait of concentration.

lesson.title: The second before
lesson.text: The pose looks relaxed. Three places give away the tension underneath.

spots.title: The stare
spots.text: The head snaps to his left. The brows are pulled together and the nostrils slightly flared. He is measuring a distance. The pupils are drilled deep so the eyes read from far below.

spots.title: The neck
spots.text: Turning the head that sharply makes a tendon stand out from collarbone to jaw. Michelangelo had dissected bodies and knew exactly which cord would tighten.

spots.title: The right hand
spots.text: The arm hangs, but look at the back of the hand: the veins are swollen. Blood is rushing there. The fingers curl around the other end of the sling.

lesson.text: So the calm is only on the surface. A hanging arm with bulging veins is like a resting cat with its ears turned: the body is at ease and ready at once. Sculptors had long known how to carve action, and how to carve rest. Carving the hinge between the two was the new thing.

The marble block was older than the sculptor. It had been cut in the quarries of Carrara around 1464, about a decade before Michelangelo was born. Two sculptors started on it and gave up, and it lay in the cathedral yard for decades, exposed to the rain.

In 1501 the cathedral workshop offered the damaged block to Michelangelo, who was 26. It was very tall, oddly shallow, and already roughed out by other hands. He had to find his figure inside what was left. That is one reason David is so slim from the side and keeps his arms close to his body.

He worked for more than two years behind a wooden fence, letting almost nobody watch. Florentines called the block “the Giant” long before it had a face. With its base the finished statue stands 5.17 m tall (about 17 ft) and weighs more than five tons.
With so little depth to work with, Michelangelo put all the movement into the outline. Compare the two sides of the body.

lines.label: The closed side
lines.text: On his right, everything hangs: straight arm, straight leg carrying the weight. This side is a quiet, nearly vertical line.

lines.label: The open side
lines.text: On his left, a zigzag: hand up at the shoulder, elbow out, hip in, knee forward, foot stepping away. This is the side the danger comes from.

lines.label: The gaze
lines.text: The eyes shoot out over the open side, past the edge of the image. The enemy is wherever that line ends. You complete the scene in your head.

lesson.text: One side at rest, one side alert, and a stare that points outside the statue: David's story is told by his body alone, with no props.

You may have sensed that the head and the right hand are too big for the body. One likely reason: the statue was ordered for a ledge high up on the cathedral, where features had to carry from the street. Another is meaning. This hero wins with his head and his hand.

It never went up there. In January 1504 a committee of some thirty citizens met to decide where to put it. Leonardo da Vinci and Botticelli were among them. The winning spot was the entrance of the town hall, in the main square. A Bible hero had become the emblem of a republic that had recently thrown out its ruling family, the Medici.

Moving the Giant about half a mile took four days and some forty men. It traveled upright, hung inside a wooden cage that rolled on greased logs. During the first night, people threw stones at it, and guards had to be posted.
More than five tons of marble balance on two ankles. Michelangelo added a discreet support. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The tree stump
spots.text: A short trunk rises behind the right leg, fused to the calf. Ancient Roman marbles used the same trick. Without it, the weight-bearing leg would likely have snapped.

lesson.text: Even with the stump, the ankles are the weak point, and fine cracks run through them today. The statue spent 369 years outdoors in sun, frost and riots. In 1527, a bench thrown from a town hall window during an uprising broke the left arm into three pieces. They were gathered up and later reattached.

In 1873 Florence finally brought David indoors, to the Accademia gallery, where a domed hall with a skylight was built around him. That is the curved vault you see overhead in this photo. A copy took his place on the square in 1910.
Indoors was not perfectly safe either. In 1991 a visitor pulled out a hammer he had hidden under his jacket and smashed a toe on the left foot before other visitors held him back.

More than five hundred years on, the arm still has not moved. Guides will tell you who wins. The statue itself never does. It keeps you exactly where Michelangelo wanted you: watching a young man decide.

quiz.question: Which moment of the story does Michelangelo show?
quiz.explanation: There is no severed head or sword: the fight has not happened yet.

quiz.question: What weapon does David carry?
options: A sling, laid over his shoulder
A short sword behind his leg
quiz.explanation: The left hand holds a sling that runs down his back to the right hand.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the block of marble?
options: It was the largest ever quarried
Other sculptors had already started on it and given up
quiz.explanation: It had been abandoned and left in the cathedral yard for decades.

quiz.question: Where was the statue first set up in 1504?
options: On a ledge of the cathedral
At the entrance of the town hall
quiz.explanation: A committee chose the entrance of the town hall on the main square.

quiz.question: What is the tree stump behind the right leg for?
options: It supports the weight of the marble
It stands for the forest where David lived
quiz.explanation: It strengthens the leg that carries most of the statue's weight.

quiz.question: Why might the head and right hand be oversized?
options: The sculptor ran out of time to correct them
The statue was meant to be seen from far below
quiz.explanation: It was ordered for a high spot on the cathedral, where features had to carry.

facts.text: Goliath's head lies at the feet of Michelangelo's David.
facts.explanation: There is no head and no sword; the giant is not shown at all.

facts.text: Leonardo da Vinci took part in the meeting that decided where the statue would stand.
facts.explanation: He sat on the 1504 committee, along with Botticelli.

facts.text: The statue has stood in a museum ever since it was finished.
facts.explanation: It stood outdoors on the main square until 1873.
